title: Abstract Factory Pattern
oneLiner: Produces whole families of related objects through one interface, guaranteeing everything it hands you is compatible.

hero.name: The Matchmaker
hero.catchphrase: One call, a whole matching set.
hero.power: Creates entire families of related objects that are guaranteed to work together.
hero.weakness: Adding a brand-new kind of product to the family means editing every factory — the family is easy to extend sideways, hard to extend with new members.
hero.origin: The Matchmaker was summoned after a UI theme bug shipped a dark-mode button next to a light-mode checkbox, because nothing enforced that widgets came from the same visual family.

story.problem: A cross-platform UI toolkit constructs `new WindowsButton()` next to `new MacCheckbox()` because each widget is created independently. Nothing stops the app from mixing platforms in the same screen.
story.solution: The Matchmaker hands out one factory per platform. Every widget it creates — button, checkbox, scrollbar — comes from the same family, so they always match.
story.result: Swapping platforms means swapping one factory. Every widget it produces is guaranteed compatible, with zero mixed-platform bugs.

before: Widgets constructed independently can mismatch platforms
No single place enforces 'this whole UI is one theme'
Adding a platform means hunting down every widget constructor
after: One factory guarantees an entire matching family
Swapping platforms is a single factory swap
Impossible to accidentally mix incompatible widgets

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A settings screen renders a Mac-style checkbox next to a Windows-style button.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: QA says our 'Windows theme' has a Mac checkbox in it. How did that even happen?

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Matchmaker appears, holding two matched sets of interlocking parts.
panels.speaker: The Matchmaker
panels.dialogue: You're picking each widget separately. Pick a FAMILY instead — I'll make sure every piece matches.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: A WindowsFactory and MacFactory appear, each implementing the same createButton()/createCheckbox() interface.
panels.speaker: The Matchmaker
panels.dialogue: Ask your factory for a button and a checkbox. Whichever factory you picked, everything it gives you belongs together.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The settings screen renders a perfectly matched Windows theme, top to bottom.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We swapped one factory and the entire screen re-themed correctly. No mismatches possible.

useWhen: Your system needs to work with multiple families of related products (themes, platforms, database drivers) that must stay internally consistent.
You want to enforce that products from one family are never mixed with another family's products.
You expect to add new families (new platforms) more often than new product types within a family.
avoidWhen: There's only ever one family of products — a plain Factory Method or direct construction is simpler.
You need to add new product types often — every factory implementation has to grow a new method, which touches every family.
The 'family' relationship is imaginary — the products don't actually need to be compatible with each other.
commonMistakes: Reaching for Abstract Factory when there's really only one product type varying (that's just Factory Method).
Forgetting that adding a new product to the family requires updating every concrete factory — an easily overlooked ripple effect.
Letting client code new() a concrete product directly 'just this once', silently breaking the family guarantee.
Confusing Abstract Factory (a family of creation methods) with Factory Method (one creation method, overridden by subclasses).
explanation.realWorldExample: Cross-platform UI toolkits (widget families per OS), database driver factories (a family of Connection/Command/Transaction objects per database engine), and cloud SDK abstractions (a family of Storage/Queue/Compute clients per provider) all use Abstract Factory.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How is this different from just calling Factory Method a few times?

conversation.speaker: The Matchmaker
conversation.message: Factory Method makes one kind of thing. I guarantee an entire compatible SET — button, checkbox, scrollbar — all from the same family, in one contract.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: What if we need a new widget type, like a slider?

conversation.speaker: The Matchmaker
conversation.message: That's my weakness — every factory has to grow a createSlider() method. Adding families is easy; adding product types touches everything.

codeBattle.scenario: Your app supports both AWS and GCP. Each cloud needs its own matching set of Storage, Queue, and Compute clients — and mixing an AWS Storage client with a GCP Queue client silently breaks auth.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Matchmaker guarantees every client you get from one cloud's factory belongs to that same cloud, eliminating cross-provider mismatches entirely.

quiz.question: What does Abstract Factory guarantee that a plain Factory Method doesn't?
options: That an entire family of related objects, not just one object, is mutually compatible
That only one instance of the factory ever exists
That objects are cloned instead of constructed
quiz.answer: That an entire family of related objects, not just one object, is mutually compatible
quiz.explanation: Abstract Factory's whole value is bundling several related creation methods so their outputs are guaranteed to match.

quiz.question: What's the main cost of using Abstract Factory?
options: Adding a new product type requires updating every concrete factory implementation
It prevents you from ever adding a new family
It requires a database connection to function
It can only create one object at a time
quiz.answer: Adding a new product type requires updating every concrete factory implementation
quiz.explanation: The family's interface is shared, so a new product method ripples across every concrete factory that implements it.

quiz.question: When is Abstract Factory overkill?
options: When there's only one family of products and no risk of mismatching them
When you have three or more platforms to support
When the products need to be related to each other
When you're building a UI toolkit
quiz.answer: When there's only one family of products and no risk of mismatching them
quiz.explanation: With a single family, there's nothing to keep consistent — a simpler factory or direct construction is enough.

quiz.question: How does Abstract Factory relate to Factory Method?
options: Abstract Factory is often implemented using several Factory Methods, one per product in the family
They are unrelated patterns that solve completely different problems
Factory Method is a special case that only works inside Abstract Factory
Abstract Factory replaces the need for interfaces entirely
quiz.answer: Abstract Factory is often implemented using several Factory Methods, one per product in the family
quiz.explanation: Each creation method on the abstract factory (createButton, createCheckbox, ...) is typically its own Factory Method under the hood.
